title: Special Array II
statement:
Call an array **special** when every two neighbouring elements in it have different parity, so each adjacent pair is one even and one odd number. A one-element array has no adjacent pairs, so it is special.

You get an integer array `nums` and a list `queries` in which `queries[i] = [from_i, to_i]` names the subarray `nums[from_i..to_i]`, both ends included. Return a boolean array `answer` of the same length as `queries`, where `answer[i]` is `true` exactly when the subarray of query `i` is special.
notes:
## Intuition

A subarray is special exactly when none of the neighbouring pairs inside it share a parity. Checking every query pair by pair costs O(length) each, up to about 10^10 steps for `10^5` long queries. Instead, mark each "bad" pair `(i - 1, i)` once and keep a running count of them: the bad pairs inside any range are then a difference of two prefix counts.

## Approach

1. Set `bad[0] = 0`. For each `i` from 1, copy `bad[i - 1]` and add 1 when `nums[i]` and `nums[i - 1]` have the same parity. Now `bad[i]` counts the bad pairs that end at indices `1..i`.
2. The pairs inside `nums[from..to]` end at indices `from + 1..to`, so `badPairs = bad[to] - bad[from]`.
3. The subarray is special exactly when `badPairs` is 0.

## Example 1, step by step

`nums = [3, 4, 1, 2, 6]`. The pairs `(3, 4)`, `(4, 1)` and `(1, 2)` mix parities, but `(2, 6)` is two even numbers, so `bad = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1]`. For the query `[0, 4]`, `badPairs = bad[4] - bad[0] = 1`, so the answer is `[false]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n + q): one pass builds `bad`, then each query is two lookups.
- Space: O(n) for `bad`, besides the output.

## Pitfalls

- Subtract `bad[from]`, not `bad[from - 1]`: the pair `(from - 1, from)` crosses the left edge and is not inside the subarray.
- A one-element query (`from === to`) has no pairs, and `bad[to] - bad[from]` is 0, so it is special.
- Re-scanning each subarray is correct but quadratic in the worst case.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `bad` | `bad[i]` = same-parity neighbouring pairs inside `nums[0..i]` |
| `i` | index of the right element of the pair being checked |
| `from`, `to` | the query's subarray bounds |
| `badPairs` | same-parity pairs inside `nums[from..to]` |
| `answer` | one boolean per query |

narration.3: Start every count at 0; bad[0] stays 0 because a single element has no pairs.
narration.4: Visit each neighbouring pair (i - 1, i) once, from left to right.
narration.5: Carry over the bad pairs counted up to index i - 1.
narration.6: Do the two neighbours have the same parity?
narration.7: Yes: this pair breaks the rule, so the running count grows by one.
narration.11: Answer each query from the prefix counts.
narration.12: The pairs inside nums[from..to] end at from + 1..to, so subtract the count up to from.
narration.13: The subarray is special exactly when it holds no bad pair.
